results.result: The authors demonstrate that 7-day treatment with PLX3397 (600 ppm) eliminates ~90-98% of microglia with scattered surviving cells throughout the brain, followed by rapid homogeneous repopulation within 3-7 days (termed GLOBAL repopulation). In contrast, 14-day treatment achieves unprecedented ~99.98% depletion with no IBA1+ cells visible across whole brain sections, and PLX3397 CNS levels remain constant between 7d and 14d treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C24 are well-supported by cited prior work (C18, C21) and current experimental data showing depletion efficiency, pharmacokinetics, and repopulation kinetics (C19, C20, C22, C24). The comparison between 7d and 14d treatments establishes the foundation for distinguishing GLOBAL from WM repopulation paradigms.

results.result: Following 14-day PLX3397 treatment and drug withdrawal, repopulating cells appear exclusively near lateral ventricles and white matter tracts by 7d recovery, spread throughout most CNS by 14d with a distinct 'wave' pattern in cortical areas, and achieve full brain coverage by 28d but at 50% lower density than controls. These WM repopulating cells display altered morphology including larger cell bodies (normalizing by 14d) and persistently reduced process length and branching complexity even at 28d recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 and C31-C33 are supported by systematic imaging data across multiple timepoints (Figure 1D, F-L) showing spatial-temporal repopulation patterns and quantitative morphological measurements. The morphological distinctions from homeostatic microglia are clearly documented and persist through 28d recovery.

results.result: WM repopulation exhibits distinct spatial-temporal dynamics compared to GLOBAL repopulation: cells first appear in precise ventricular/WM locations (SVZ, corpus callosum, RMS) rather than homogeneously throughout the brain, then migrate in radial and tangential patterns through four defined stages, initially filling WM and caudoputamen before breaking through WM tract barriers to spread through cortex in a dynamic wave between 7-14d recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C45 are supported by comprehensive spatial heat map analysis (Figure 2A-C) and detailed stage-by-stage characterization of the migratory wave (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The contrast with GLOBAL repopulation (C34) and the sequential staging (C40-C45) provide clear evidence for this distinct repopulation pattern.

results.result: Proliferation during WM repopulation is spatially restricted to ventricles/WM tracts initially and remains localized within the migrating wavefront (~100-150 µm width), with cells ceasing proliferation once behind the wave, contrasting with the distributed proliferation pattern of GLOBAL repopulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by Ki67 immunostaining data (Figure 2E-G) showing proliferation patterns that differ fundamentally from GLOBAL repopulation. The wavefront-specific proliferation and its cessation in the wake provide mechanistic insight into the repopulation dynamics.

results.result: Following 14-day PLX3397 treatment, approximately 15 surviving IBA1+ cells (~0.02% of control, 99.98% depletion) are found exclusively in SVZ and adjacent WM areas. These surviving cells lack canonical microglial markers (P2RY12-, TMEM119-) and display distinct morphology, but eventually succumb to CSF1Ri after 3.5 months of continuous treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by extensive stereological quantification throughout the brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and marker characterization (Figure 3E-G). The 3.5-month data (C52) demonstrates these cells are not permanently resistant but have delayed susceptibility to CSF1Ri.

results.result: Surviving SVZ/WM myeloid cells and WM repopulating cells share characteristics with previously described SVZ microglia, including amoeboid morphology, activated phenotype, and initially low/absent P2RY12 and TMEM119 expression, though repopulating cells acquire these markers by 28d recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by citations to prior literature (C53, C54) and current immunostaining data showing temporal marker expression (Figure 3H-I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). The acquisition of microglial markers over time suggests phenotypic plasticity of these cells.

results.result: Transcriptional profiling reveals that early WM repopulating cells (7d recovery) upregulate genes involved in myeloid activation/priming and monocyte-macrophage signaling rather than homeostatic microglial genes, while 28d recovery cells show increased expression of MHC components and priming genes. Once migrated from SVZ, WM repopulated cells become susceptible to CSF1Ri treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by Nanostring gene expression analysis (Figure 3K-L) and CSF1Ri re-treatment experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I-K). The transcriptional data clearly distinguishes WM repopulating cells from homeostatic microglia, and the re-treatment data demonstrates their CSF1R-dependence once outside the SVZ niche.

results.result: In H2K-BCL2 mice (which overexpress the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2 in hematopoietic cells), 14-day PLX3397 treatment achieves only 61-95% microglial elimination, and subsequent recovery produces GLOBAL rather than WM repopulation. This demonstrates that WM repopulation requires >99% depletion rather than being a drug-specific effect, and that CSF1Ri-induced death is caspase-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by experimental data in BCL2 transgenic mice (Figure 4) and citations to prior work on BCL2 function (C61, C62) and CSF1Ri mechanism (C63). The genetic rescue experiment provides strong evidence that depletion level, not drug treatment duration, determines repopulation mode.

results.result: Between 3-5d recovery, WM repopulating cells transiently express precursor/progenitor markers NESTIN (92% at 5d), MASH1 (81% at 5d), and TIE2 (50% at 5d), but are consistently negative for GFAP, DCX, OLIG2, and SOX2 throughout recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 are supported by systematic immunostaining across multiple timepoints (Figure 5A-B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The transient expression of certain markers and consistent absence of others helps characterize the phenotype of repopulating cells, though the functional significance of transient marker expression requires further investigation.

results.result: Lineage tracing experiments demonstrate that WM repopulating cells do not derive from Ascl1+ or Nestin+ progenitors despite transiently expressing these markers. Using Cx3cr1CreERT2 mice (accounting for 8-12% leaky Cre expression), 95% of repopulating cells at 7d recovery express YFP, indicating they derive from a Cx3cr1+ cell source.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are supported by lineage tracing experiments using multiple Cre driver lines (Figure 5C-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The acknowledgment and quantification of Cre leakiness (C74) strengthens confidence in the Cx3cr1 lineage tracing results. The negative results with Ascl1 and Nestin Cre lines effectively rule out these progenitor populations.

results.result: WM repopulating cells first appear between 3-7d recovery in the SVZ (specifically the αSVZ and posterior RMS), then accumulate in anatomically connected WM regions (corpus callosum, RMS, olfactory bulb, internal capsule, cerebral peduncle) before filling grey matter. These anatomical niches and migration patterns recapitulate microglial colonization during embryonic/postnatal brain development.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 are supported by detailed anatomical analysis (Figure 5F-H) and citations to developmental studies (C82-C84). The parallel between WM repopulation and developmental colonization is compelling and suggests reactivation of developmental programs. Claim C81 about anatomical connectivity is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis of micro-dissected SVZ tissue identifies 227 DEGs between control and 5d recovery, with GO analysis highlighting myeloid cell differentiation, leukocyte activation, and chemotaxis pathways. Homeostatic microglial genes (P2ry12, Siglech, Trem2) are downregulated while chemokines (particularly Ccl12) are highly upregulated. CCL12 neutralization significantly reduces repopulating cell numbers at 7d recovery without affecting migration distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 are supported by bulk RNA-seq data from micro-dissected SVZ (Figure 6A-D) and functional validation via antibody neutralization (Figure 6E-H). The CCL12 neutralization experiment provides causal evidence for this chemokine's role in early repopulation, though the specific mechanism (proliferation vs. survival) remains uncertain as noted in C90.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence rule out peripheral cell contribution to WM repopulation: choroid plexus macrophages don't repopulate until 14d despite adjacent parenchymal repopulation; WM repopulating cells are CCR2-; bone marrow progenitors expand rather than suppress with CSF1Ri; and CX3CR1/CCR2 double knockout shows normal WM repopulation. In Ccl2-/- mice, incomplete depletion (~90-95%) results in GLOBAL rather than WM repopulation, confirming >99% depletion is required for WM repopulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 are supported by multiple complementary approaches (Figure 7A-D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The convergent evidence from different experimental systems (CCR2 reporter mice, knockout mice, bone marrow analysis) strongly supports the conclusion that peripheral cells do not contribute. The Ccl2 KO data (C96-C98) provides additional genetic evidence for the depletion threshold requirement.

results.result: Head-shielded bone marrow chimera experiments definitively demonstrate that WM repopulating cells do not derive from peripheral BM-derived cells. In chimeric mice with GFP+ bone marrow, no GFP+ cells appear in control brain parenchyma (only in choroid plexus), 14d PLX3397 eliminates all myeloid cells, and repopulating IBA1+ cells at 7-14d recovery are GFP-, ruling out BM contribution including from choroid plexus macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C105 are supported by rigorous bone marrow chimera experiments with head-shielded irradiation (Figure 7E-K). This is the gold standard approach for determining cell origin, and the negative result (GFP- repopulating cells) provides definitive evidence against peripheral contribution. The experimental design appropriately controls for BBB disruption by using head-shielding.

results.result: RNA-seq of FACS-sorted CD11b+CD45int cells at 28d recovery reveals 69 DEGs compared to control microglia (vs. only 25 DEGs in GLOBAL repopulation), with GO enrichment for cellular component size regulation, amoeboid migration, and wound healing. WM repopulating cells show robust enrichment of DAM/WAM-associated genes (Clec7a, Axl, Apoe, Cst7, Ctsd, Ly9) and reduced Sall1 expression. AXL and CLEC7A protein expression is detected in repopulating cells but not controls. Time-series analysis reveals differential LPS responses between control and repopulating cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C114 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq analysis of sorted cells (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) with appropriate statistical thresholds (logFC >1, FDR <0.05). The comparison to GLOBAL repopulation strengthens the conclusion that WM cells are distinct. Immunostaining validation of key markers (C110) and LPS challenge experiments (C106, C113) provide functional context. The conclusion (C114) appropriately synthesizes the transcriptional and functional data.

results.result: Behavioral testing of 28d recovery mice reveals reduced locomotion and impaired novel place recognition, but no other significant cognitive or behavioral deficits. Live two-photon imaging shows WM repopulating cells respond to laser injury with similar migration rates as control microglia and display similar process motility, though with fewer and thicker processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 are supported by systematic behavioral testing (Figure 9A-H) and live imaging experiments (Figure 9I-L, Videos 1-2). The behavioral battery is comprehensive, and the modest deficits (C115-C116) are appropriately qualified by the lack of other changes (C117). The live imaging provides functional validation that repopulating cells can respond to injury despite their altered morphology.

results.result: WM repopulating cells regulate perineuronal nets (PNNs) similarly to homeostatic microglia, as PNN staining increases during 14d depletion but returns to normal by 28d recovery. Unlike developmental WM microglia that participate in myelinogenesis, 28d recovery mice show no changes in Olig2+ or PDGFRα+ cells, though there is a non-significant trend toward decreased MBP staining suggesting possible myelin debris clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are supported by PNN staining data (Figure 9M-N) and prior work citation. Claims C123-C125 regarding oligodendrocyte markers and myelin are supported by immunostaining (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), though C125 appropriately notes the lack of statistical significance and speculative nature of the MBP clearance interpretation.

results.result: At 3 months recovery, WM repopulating cells maintain reduced density and amoeboid-like morphology (larger cell bodies, fewer/shorter processes). Transcriptional differences persist with continued P2ry12 downregulation and Clec7a upregulation. GO analysis shows upregulated DEGs involve neuron projection development, axon guidance, and synaptic transmission, suggesting potential roles in axonal homeostasis. These sustained differences indicate WM repopulating cells represent a distinct myeloid population rather than delayed microglial maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C131 are supported by long-term morphological analysis (Figure 10C-F) and bulk tissue RNA-seq (Figure 10H-J). The persistence of phenotypic and transcriptional differences at 3 months strongly supports the conclusion (C131) that these are distinct cells rather than slowly maturing microglia. However, the interpretation about axonal homeostasis (C130) is speculative based on GO terms and would benefit from functional validation.

results.result: Background claims establishing microglial biology: microglia constitute 5-10% of adult CNS cells, perform immune defense and tissue maintenance functions, arise from yolk sac erythromyeloid progenitors that colonize the brain at E8.5-E9.5 via meninges/ventricles, first populate white matter then migrate to cortical plate, and mature by P28 expressing canonical markers (P2ry12, Tmem119, Siglech, Cx3cr1, Olfml3, Fcrls, Sall1).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are standard background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide necessary context for the experimental work but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Background on microglial heterogeneity: recent scRNA-seq studies have identified disease-associated (DAM, MGnD), injury-responsive (IRM), and region/stage-specific (PAM, ATM, WAM) microglial populations. WAMs in corpus callosum share DAM gene signatures including phagocytosis genes and increase with aging/disease. PAMs/ATMs in developing corpus callosum share location and phagocytic profiles with WAMs. Adult homeostatic microglia appear less heterogeneous.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 accurately summarize recent literature on microglial diversity with appropriate citations. These establish the conceptual framework for interpreting WM repopulating cells as related to WAMs/PAMs/ATMs.

results.result: Background on microglial homeostasis: microglia are maintained by TGF-β, IL-34, and CSF1 signaling; are long-lived and self-renewing even after 80-95% depletion; but no approach has achieved complete depletion to date.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by citations to prior literature and establish the rationale for developing improved depletion methods. Claim C17 is contradicted by the current study's achievement of 99.98% depletion, which is the key advance.

results.result: Within 14-21 days of GLOBAL repopulation, repopulating microglia attain similar densities, morphologies, marker expression, gene expression, and LPS responses as resident microglia.
results.evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by citations to the authors' prior publications establishing the characteristics of GLOBAL repopulation. This provides important context for distinguishing WM repopulation as a distinct phenomenon.
